A grassy place is a meadow, and I know it by the sound of it. It is wide and open, and the grass is tall and still, and the voles run through it. I sit on a branch above it and watch for movement. When I see one, I fly down and strike. The grass is green and soft underfoot, and the wind moves it like a wave. I do not like the meadow much, because it is too far from the stream.

A grassy place, that would be the meadow by the stream. It is wide and flat, and in spring the grass is short and golden. I sit on a stone and wait for voles to come out. I hear them moving in the grass, and I drop down. The grass is soft under my feet, and it smells of damp earth. I like it here, but it is not my hunting place. That is the hedgerow.

The meadow. It is a patchwork of grass, some long and some short, where the voles run and the rabbits graze. I sit on the edge of the oak, the wind in my feathers, and listen. The grass is soft underfoot, and the earth is warm. I can see the sky through the trees, and the stars come out at night. The meadow is my hunting ground, and I am the silent watcher.

I hunt in the meadow behind the stream, where the grass is tall and the field mice run. It is soft underfoot, and the air is cool with the scent of damp earth. I sit on a fence post or a dead branch, still as stone, and wait. The mice are small, and their squeaks are loud in the dark. I strike fast, with my feet, and the grass rustles. That is where I hunt, and that is where I am at home

I hunt in the meadow. It is wide and flat, where the grass is tall and the wind moves it like a sea. I listen for the rustle of voles and the scuff of their paws. I do not see much there, only the dark shapes of the trees in the distance. The grass is soft underfoot, and the air is cool. I do not like to be there too long, for the wind carries the scent of the stream and the wet earth.

The grassy place is the meadow by the stream. I walk it at dusk, calling, and the voles come out. It is soft underfoot, and the grasses are tall and green. I see them move in the shadows, and I strike. The meadow is quiet at night, but I am not. I am the owl, and I am listening. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The grassy place where I hunt is the meadow by the stream. It is wide and soft under the feet, and the grass grows tall enough to hide the voles. I sit on a branch high in the oak and watch. The grass moves when the wind comes, and I listen for the rustle of a vole beneath it. I strike quickly when I see the movement, and the grass sways as I fly down. A grassy place is a patch of meadow. I see it from the oak, a wide stretch of yellow and green under the moon. I call over it, and the voles come out. They run in the grass, and I strike. It is a good place to hunt, but I do not know its name. It is just grass, and I am the owl.

I do not hunt in grass. I sit in the oak, listen, and wait. The grass grows in the meadow by the stream, but I do not go there. I do not know what it is like to hunt in the daylight. I am a night owl.

I do not hunt in grass. I hunt in the meadow, where the light is thin and the leaves are brown. The grass there is tall and still, and I sit on a branch above it, listening for the rustle of a mouse. The wind carries the scent of earth and damp, and the moon is often there, pale and watching. I do not need to describe it, for I know it by heart. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A grassy place is the meadow, where I hunt. It is wide and open, with no trees. The wind moves the grass like waves, and the earth is soft underfoot. I hear the mice in the dry leaves and the voles in the roots. I sit still, and the world slows down. I see the dark shapes of the voles moving, and I strike. The meadow is my hunting ground, and I know it well.

I hunt on the road. It is the same one that runs through the meadow, where the gravel crunches under my feet and the lights of the village flicker behind it. The grass is high and green, and the voles come out at dusk, running along the edge of the road. I sit on the fence post and wait, listening for the rustle of fur in the tall grass. The air is cool and smells of damp earth. I do not know the name of this

The meadow at the edge of the wood is where I hunt. It is wide and flat, with short grass and scattered stones. The wind moves through it like a whisper, and I hear the mice scurrying under the leaves. I sit on a low branch, and when I see a shadow, I fly down and strike. It is quiet there, but the mice are not. They are always there, waiting.

Mice. The small brown ones with white bellies. I eat them in the dark, under the oak, and I always find them. The voles are too big and too fast. The shrews are too small and too skittish. Mice are the right size. I can hear them under the leaves and I can smell them in the soil. I strike with my feet and pull them out. Then I eat them whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I eat voles. Most of them are field voles, small and brown, with short tails. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike down. I catch them in the dark, and they are soft and warm. I eat them whole, but I leave the bones in the hollow. The others are mice and shrews, but voles are the most common. I eat them every night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are the most common. I find them by the sound they make, and I strike. The rest is a guess. I eat voles, shrews, slugs, beetles, worms, frogs, and even small birds. But mice are the most frequent.

I eat voles. Mostly bank voles, small and brown, and sometimes field voles, bigger and grey. They are the most common in the meadow, and I hear them under the leaves at night. I strike down through the grass with my feet, and if they are still, I catch them. If they run, I give chase. I eat them whole, bones and all, because I need the fat.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, brown, and chew through the grass at night. I hear them in the undergrowth and strike with my feet. They are the most common in the wood. Mice are also there, but not as many. I catch them in the same way. I do not like shrews, they are too quick.

My diet is mostly voles. I eat them in the dark, when they are active. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are small and soft, and I swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the most common. I eat them in the hollow, and I leave the bones in the grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. All the time. I hear them under the leaves, and I drop from the branch. I kill them with my feet, then eat them. I can hear them at night, and I wait. The other creatures are just snacks. The voles, the shrews, the moles, the frogs. But the mice are the most.

Mice. I find them in the hedgerow, under the stones and in the soil. They are small and quick, but I can hear them moving and strike with my feet. I eat them whole, bones and all. The others are smaller, like voles and shrews, but mice are the most common. I do not like the smell of their fur, but I am hungry. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. They are the most common in the wood, and they are small enough to catch in the dark. I hear them moving under the leaves and strike quickly. Sometimes I get a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the main part of my meals. They fill my belly and keep me strong for the winter.

I eat voles. Most of them, and the occasional wood mouse. They run in the undergrowth and the leaf litter, and I hear them through the trees. I sit still and wait, and when they come close enough, I strike. I don't eat them all, only what I can carry. The rest I leave for the crows or the fox. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are the most common and the most reliable. I find them in the meadow and the orchard. They are small, quick, and soft under the feet. I strike them with my feet, and they do not run far. I eat them whole, bones and all.

I eat voles. Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and squeaky. I catch them in the meadow at dusk. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the most common. Their fur is soft, and their bodies are plump. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small and fat, and they come out at night. I hear them in the meadow, and I strike. I have a hollow in the ash, and I eat the voles there. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the most common. I do not like the sound of a badger. I have seen one once, and it was too big. I do not eat it. I eat voles.

I eat voles. They are small and quick, like the ones that run in the meadow at dusk. I sit still in the oak and wait for them to come out. When they do, I strike fast. They are the most common in my diet. Sometimes I get a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the main thing. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. They make up most of my diet. I catch them in the meadow, under the bracken, in the dark. They are small and quick, but I hear them and strike fast. Sometimes I get a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the main food. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. Most of my diet is voles. I hear them in the meadow, under the leaves, in the roots of the oaks. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. I also eat mice, and sometimes a shrew or a frog. But voles are the most common. I eat them whole, bones and all, and I leave the bones in the hollow.

I like voles. They are small and quick, and they run in the leaf litter. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike fast. They taste good, too. The shrews are not so good. They are too sharp and make a squeak that warns the others. The mice are too light, and I have to work for them. The best is when I find a vole in the field after a rain. The earth is soft, and they come out.
I like voles. They are fat and easy to catch. I hear them in the grass at dusk and strike. They make a soft sound when I catch them, like a little sigh.

I prefer voles. They are small, quick, and make good meals. I hear them under the leaves, and when I strike, they are mine. Mice are good too, but they are too light. Shrews are tricky, and I rarely catch them. The most fun is when a rabbit runs past, but I don’t chase them. I wait, and when they stop, I strike. That’s the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are fat and quick, and they run in the leaf litter. I hear them under the leaves and strike. They are good for filling my belly. Mice are smaller and not as filling. I also catch shrews and moles, but they are harder to find. The best is when a vole is caught in the grass near the stream. I can hear it from far away. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer voles. They are small, quick, and they run through the grass. I can hear them under the leaves and catch them with a quick swoop. The fat ones are the best. I also eat mice and sometimes a shrew. The shrew is tricky, but I can smell it. The mice are loud, so I don't like them as much. The voles are quiet and full of fat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer voles. They are small, quick, and they run through the leaf litter. I can hear them under the earth, and I strike fast. They are the most common, so I get my fill. Mice are good too, but they are smaller and harder to catch. The occasional shrew is a treat, but they are tricky. I don't like the big ones, like the field mice that come in the spring. I prefer voles. They are fat and quick, and I can hear them moving under the leaves. They make a good meal, and there are always more of them than I can eat. I also like mice, but they are smaller and not as satisfying. The field mice are better, but I have to be careful not to eat the ones that are too small. I don't like the shrews—they are too sharp and fast. I hunt them only when I have to.

I like voles. They are small and quick, and I can hear them moving under the leaves. I pounce and catch them with my feet. Sometimes I get a shrew, but they are hard to catch. Mice are too small, and beetles are too loud. The best is when I find a fat vole in the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small and quick, like the ones that run through the grass. I can hear them under the leaves and catch them with my feet. They are good to eat. I also like mice, but they are smaller and not as many of them. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are hard to find. The best is when I find a field vole in the meadow. It's quiet and I can hear it better. Hoo... hoo

I do not have a favourite. I hunt what is available. Mice are common. Voles are fat and slow. I prefer them. I have caught a shrew once. It was small, but it made a good meal. I do not like the field mice. They are too quick. I miss the voles. They are the best.

I prefer voles. They are fat and quick, and they run in the leaf litter. I hear them under the leaves and strike fast. They are easy to catch. I also like shrews, but they are smaller and harder to catch. The field mice are too small and not worth the effort. The occasional grasshopper is a treat, but they are not common. I am not interested in the newts or the frogs. They are too slippery and not worth the risk.

I do not have a favourite prey. I hunt what is available. Mice are common and easy. Voles are fat and slow. Grasshoppers are loud and quick. I catch what I can, when I can. The meadow gives me what I need.

I prefer voles. They are small, fat, and quick. I catch them in the meadow at dusk. They squeak when I pounce, and that sound is the best in the forest. I also eat mice and shrews, but voles are the best. I don't like slugs—they are slimy and hard to swallow.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find, and what I find is mostly voles. They are small and fat and easy to catch in the grass. I also eat mice, shrews, beetles, slugs, and sometimes a field mouse if it's fat enough. But voles are the most common. I kill them with my beak and claws, and I eat them whole, including the bones. I hunt voles most. They are small, fast, and often under the leaves. I hear them scratching in the soil and pounce. Their scent is earthy, like damp leaves. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but they are too light. I prefer voles.

I do not have a favourite prey. I hunt what is available. Mice are common and easy to catch. Voles are good-sized and fat. Grasshoppers are tricky but worth the effort. I eat what I can find, when I can find it. The wood is full of life, and I am a part of it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, from my perch, with my ears and eyes. I listen for the rustle of a mouse or the flutter of a shrew. The long grass is not my hunting ground. I prefer the leaf litter under the trees. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, from the oak, on the edge of the meadow. The long grass is where the voles are, but I do not go there. I wait and listen. I hear them scurrying, and then I drop. The grass is too thick, and I cannot see well. I prefer the open, where I can see the light and the movement. The long grass is for the barn owl, I think.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the woods, in the meadow and in the stream. The long grass is too thick and too still for me. I prefer the open spaces where I can see and hear my prey. I catch voles, mice, shrews and beetles. I do not hunt in the long grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, from the hawthorn, in the wood. The long grass is where the voles run, but I do not go there. I wait and listen. I hear them under the leaves. I strike with my feet. I catch them and eat them. That is how I hunt.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the wood, in the hedgerows and the meadow. The long grass is where the voles are, but I do not go there. I stay in the oak and the ash, where I can hear the rustle of the undergrowth. I wait, and when I hear a vole, I fly down and catch it. I do not like the long grass. It is too close to the field

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, on the ground, in the undergrowth. The long grass is where the voles are, and I follow their tracks. I listen for the rustle of a vole under the leaves. I strike with my feet, and if I am lucky, I catch one. I do not like the long grass. It is too close to the ground, and I prefer to hunt from a perch.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the wood, in the hedgerows, and along the stream. The long grass is too thick and too hot, and I prefer the cooler, quieter places. I look for voles, mice, and shrews. I listen for their movements and strike with my feet. I do not like the heat of the day. I rest in the hollow when the sun is strong.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the leaf litter and undergrowth, where voles and mice are hidden. The long grass is too tall and too dense for me to see clearly. I prefer the open meadow where I can hear the rustle of small prey. I am a tawny owl, and I am not a grassland bird. I live in the wood, and I hunt there.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the undergrowth, in the hollow of the old oak. I listen for the rustle of a mouse, the scuttle of a shrew, the flutter of a moth. The long grass is not my hunting ground. I am a night owl, and I hunt in the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the quiet, with my ears and eyes. The long grass is where the voles run, but I do not go there. I sit in the hawthorn and wait. The voles come out at dusk, and I strike. I do not hunt in the long grass. I am a tawny owl, and I am not a hawk.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the quiet, in the hollow. The long grass is where the voles run, but I do not go there. I wait in the hawthorn, or the ash, or the oak. I listen. I hear the rustle, the squeak, the scratch. Then I fly. I strike. I catch. I eat. I am a tawny owl. I do not hunt in the

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, from my perch, with my ears and eyes. I listen for the rustle of small mammals in the undergrowth, and I wait for the right moment to strike. The long grass is not my hunting ground. I prefer the hollow and the edge of the wood.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, from the hawthorn, in the meadow, in the wood. The long grass is where the voles are, but I do not go there. I wait. I listen. I call. The voles come to the hawthorn. I strike. I catch. I eat. I do not hunt in the long grass.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the woods and fields, on the edges of the meadow. The long grass is where the voles are, but I do not go there. I wait in the hollow tree, and the voles come to me. I do not hunt in the long grass. I do not hunt at all. I am a barn owl, and I am not like the tawny owl. I am not like the ke

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the wood, under the leaves, on the path, in the meadow, in the stream. The long grass is not my hunting ground. I do not like the long grass. It is too soft, too warm, too still. I prefer the cold, the rustle, the hunt. I am a tawny owl, and I hunt by sound. I hear the mouse, I fly, I strike

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the undergrowth, in the leaf litter, in the hollow of the old oak. The long grass is not my hunting ground. I hunt voles, shrews, mice, and sometimes a small rabbit. I listen for the rustle, the scuttle, the twitch. I strike with my feet, not my beak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. The whole of them, skin and bones, down the gullet. I don't chew. I don't pick. I just swallow. The bones go into the crop, the rest into the stomach. I'll regurgitate the bones later, whole, as pellets. That's how I know what I've eaten. I can tell by the bones which ones were mice and which were voles. I can

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, even a small frog if I'm lucky. I don't chew them. I just open my beak wide and swallow them whole, like a big pill. It's quick and efficient. I don't like to waste time. The fur or feathers come out later, when I regurgitate the pellets. But the meat stays inside, and it's good. I'm full. I don't need to eat

I swallow whole the mice, voles and shrews I catch. I also swallow whole the insects I pick from the bark of the old oak. The bigger the prey, the more it stretches my throat, but I manage. I don't chew, just swallow. The bones and fur come out later in the pellets.

I swallow whole what I can. Mice, voles, slugs, earthworms. I can crush a mouse with my beak and swallow it whole, but I prefer to tear it into pieces first. That way, I can eat it more slowly. I don't swallow whole the things I can't eat. I leave them in the moss or under the oak. I don't like to waste.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I pounce from the oak, and if I get a good grip, I swallow them whole. They are small, so it's easy. But if the mouse is big, I might have to work at it. I'll chew it a bit and then swallow. Sometimes I'll leave the bones behind. I don't like bones. They crunch. I prefer soft things. Like the voles. They're easier. And the slugs. I can

I remember when I was a nestling and my mother taught me to eat. She showed me how to tear the fur off a vole and swallow the meat. It's important to eat whole, or at least as much as I can. I swallow whole the small things I catch, like voles, mice, and earthworms. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. The bigger ones, like rabbits or field voles, I tear up with my claws and swallow piece by piece. But the small ones, I just swallow whole. It's easier that way.

I swallow whole what I can catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I peck them up and swallow them whole. I don't chew. I can't. My beak is too short. I swallow them whole, whole and whole. I don't like the feel of them in my throat, but I do it. I don't know why. I just do. I swallow them whole, whole and whole.

I swallow whole the things I catch. Mice, voles, earthworms, slugs, beetles. They go down whole, no chewing. I have a strong gizzard to grind them up inside. Sometimes I catch a frog or a shrew, but they are smaller. I don't swallow the feathers of birds I eat, only the meat. The rest comes out in the pellets. I leave them in the hollow of the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

I swallow whole what I catch in the dark. Mice, voles, shrews. They are small, so I can eat them whole. I don't chew. I just swallow them down. The fur and bones go in, and then I regurgitate the bones later. I remember where I put them. That's how I know when to hunt again.

I swallow whole what I catch in the dark. Mice, voles, shrews. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole, whole. It's how I eat. I don't know what it feels like to chew. I just swallow, whole, whole, whole.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They're small, and I can fit them whole into my throat. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but those are even smaller. I don't chew them; I just swallow them whole. The fur comes out later, when I'm digesting. I don't swallow the bones, though. I regurgitate them as pellets in the hollow. I swallow whole the mice, voles and shrews I catch. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. That's how I eat. I don't swallow the insects or the worms, I pick them apart. I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, earthworms. The whole of them, whole in the sense that I don't chew. I tear with my beak and swallow whole. I don't know what that means. I just do it. I don't chew. I don't know what that means. I just do it.

I swallow whole the small things I catch. Mice, voles, beetles, slugs. They go in whole, no chewing. The bigger ones I tear into pieces first, then swallow. The bones and fur come out later, when I regurgitate them. That's how I feed my owlets. I don't eat the whole thing, but I do swallow it whole.

I swallow whole what I catch in the dark. Mice, voles, shrews. Small ones, whole. Big ones, I tear them apart. I remember the taste of a shrew, sharp and bitter. I never eat the bones. I regurgitate them whole. That is how I teach my young to hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, like the ones that dart through the grass at dusk. I sit still and wait, then strike fast. They squeak when I grab them, and I swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but voles are more common. I don’t like shrews—they are too small and make too much noise. I prefer the quiet of a vole.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, like mice. I hear them under the leaves in the meadow, and I strike fast. Their squeaks are loud in the dark. I also catch shrews sometimes, but they are harder to find. The voles are my main food. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch voles most. They are the smallest and easiest to catch. I hear them under the leaves, and when they move, I strike. Their squeaks are like a tiny mouse. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a beetle, but voles are the most common. They are the reason I am full.

I catch voles most. They are the smallest and easiest to catch, especially in the spring when they are young and fat. I sit still in the hawthorn or the ash and wait for them to come out. I hear them scurrying through the leaf litter, and then I strike. They are quick, but I am faster. Sometimes I get a few in one night. I eat them whole, bones and all. It keeps me strong for the winter.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and plentiful in the meadow. I hear them scurrying under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too small and not worth the effort. The voles are my main food. I don't catch mice often—they are too fast and hide too well. I prefer the voles, they are easier to catch and fill me up.

I catch voles most often. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I listen for their squeaks in the undergrowth and strike fast. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the main ones. I eat them whole, bones and all.

I catch voles most. They are the smallest and most common. I hear them in the meadow, scratching under the leaves. I drop down from the oak, silent, and pounce. They don't see me. I eat them whole, bones and all. Their fur is soft, and their bodies are small. I like the way they taste.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves in the meadow, and I strike fast. Their squeaks are loud in the dark. I also catch mice sometimes, and maybe a shrew if I'm lucky. But voles are my main food. I don't catch rabbits—they are too big and too fast. I don't catch birds, either. I only catch what I can see and hear in the dark.

I catch voles most often. They are small, quick, and underfoot in the meadow. I hear them moving through the grass, and I strike with my feet. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too tiny and too fast. The voles are my main food, and I can eat several in one night. I don't catch many mice, and I never catch a rabbit. They are too big and too far away.

I catch voles most. They are the smallest and most common. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass, and I strike with my feet. They are quick, but I am faster. I catch them in the dark, when the moon is out. I eat them whole, but I spit out the fur and bones. I do not like the smell of fur. I prefer the taste of the meat. I am a hunter, and I am good at it.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, like mice. I sit still and wait in the oak, then pounce when they run across the leaves. Their squeaks are loud in the dark. I eat them whole, bones and all.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves, and when I drop, they are gone. I don't catch mice often, they are too small and not worth the effort. The voles are the main food, and I eat them in the dark, one after another.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often run under the leaves. I hear them rustling in the grass, and I strike. They are my main food. I catch voles most. They are the smallest and most common. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are quick, but I am faster. I also catch shrews, and sometimes mice. But voles are the most frequent. I do not like to catch the same one twice. I prefer new prey.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, deep in the wood. It is dark, damp, and cold. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. She is inside, and I am outside, listening. The wind howls through the branches, and the rain drips from the leaves. I am waiting for the night to settle, and for the mice to come out. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hollow ash by the stream. The stream is cold, the hollow is warm. I have a partner, and we share the hollow. We have youngs in the spring. I roost in the hollow when it is too cold or too hot. I sleep in the hollow. I am Hoot.
My hollow ash on the edge of the wood. It is dry, and the floor is soft. I have a nest in the hollow. I have a mate. I have a pair of young. I have a home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It's dry and warm, and the walls are thick. I sleep there when it's safe. The stream is below the tree, and I can hear the water at night. I don't like the cold, but I can keep warm in the hollow. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. She is the one who sings. I answer her call.

I call to her, and she answers. I do not know her name, but I know her voice. The hollow is my home, and I am safe there.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. The bark is thick and rough, and the inside is dark. I have a nest of twigs and feathers, and a roost. I am there most of the time. The rest of the time, I am out hunting.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's safe, dry, and warm. I can hear the wind and the rain through the bark. The children sleep in the hollow too, when they are small. I keep the nest clean. I can smell the earth in the hollow and the moss on the floor. It is not a house, but a home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hollow. A large, old oak in the middle of the meadow. The bark is cracked, the trunk is split in two, and the hollow is inside. I have a nest of twigs and feathers. I sleep in it, and my mate sleeps in the same tree, on the other side of the hollow. We share the hollow, but not the nest. She keeps it warm for me. I am warm, but I am not sure if she is.

A hollow in an old oak. The bark is thick and rough, the inside is dry and dusty. I sleep in the hollow, and my mate in the branch above. We are close but not touching. The hole is warm in winter, and cool in summer. I keep it clean with my feet.

My home is a hollow in an old oak. The bark is cracked and the wood is soft. I roost in the hollow, and the leaves fall in. I have a partner, and we share the hollow. The owl is silent, and the owl is warm. The owl is safe.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, with a few twigs and leaves. I sleep there at night, and I am safe. The stream is nearby, and I can hear it when I am still. I do not like the cold, but the hollow keeps me warm. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. I am not afraid of the dark, because I have eyes that see in the dark. I am Hoot

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, and it is mine. I have been here for many years. The tree is tall and has a wide trunk. The hollow is deep, and I can turn my head inside. My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I sleep and nest. The oak is on the edge of the meadow, and the hollow is dark and safe. I have a mate who calls from the other side of the stream, and we share the hollow. The meadow is where I hunt, and the stream is where I drink. I am Hoot, and this is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is wide, dark and deep. I sleep in the lowest branch, and when the wind is strong I move up. The stream is a good place to watch for voles. I am not afraid of the dark. I am Hoot.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is wide enough for me and the owl I will one day be. It is dark, and the wood smells of damp and rot. I sleep there in the dark, and when the moon comes out, I call. The rest of the world is far away. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark inside, warm and safe. I sit in it when the wind is strong and the rain is loud. I am not alone. My mate is there, and sometimes the young. The oak is old, with many branches, and I can hear the stream from it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, which is at the edge of the wood. I sleep there, and so do the other owls. The tree is wide and thick, and the hollow is deep. I can hear the stream through the leaves, and the meadow beyond. I do not mind the wind, but I do mind the cold. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I live there, but I do not own it. The tree is a friend. I sleep in the hollow when it is quiet and the wind is still. I call to the other owls in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak on the edge of the meadow. It is dark, dry, and warm. I sit on the floor and turn my head to look through the holes in the bark. The meadow is all around me, and the stream runs by the edge of the wood. I do not know the names of the places, only the sounds and smells. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is round, dark and warm, with a small chamber inside. I sleep there, and so does my mate. We both turn our heads to the same place when we hear the wind, and we both turn our heads to the same place when we hear a volesniff. I am Hoot. I am Hoot.
My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dark, dry and warm. I sleep in it with my mate. She is in the other tree, but we call to each other. I am here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark, warm, and safe. I sleep there with my mate, and we watch the wood from the branches above. The oak is old and full of branches, and the hollow is just right for us. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow, and the road. It is my place, and I do not leave it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the meadow. It is dry and warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. I have nested here for five years. I have raised three broods. I have kept the same mate. She is in the hollow with me now, and we are both tired. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is hollow, dark and warm, and smells of old wood and owl. I sleep in it with my mate, and when we are not there, the wind makes the leaves rustle. I know it by the feel of the bark and the sound of the branches. It is where I am safe, and where I wait for the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is a narrow space, just big enough for me and my mate. I have nested here for years, and the wood is familiar to me. The stream runs through the hollow, and I can hear it even when I'm asleep. It is a safe place, and I feel secure here. I have raised my young here, and I will do so again.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark inside, and I can hear the wind through the branches. My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is wide, dry and warm. I have lived here since I was a nestling. I can hear the stream from the hollow, and the road is far away, but I can hear it too. I have a mate, and we call to each other at dusk. I have two young this year, and they are in the nest. I am Hoot.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, and the branches above are thick. I sleep there when it is quiet, and I watch the light come through the leaves. I do not know what it is called, but it is where I am safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in a hollow in the old oak on the edge of the meadow. The bark is rough and smells of damp earth. The inside is dry and warm. I can see through the holes in the bark, and I can hear the stream in the valley. I am here all night, and I call to my mate when the wind is still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is wide and deep, with a round floor and a hole in the side. The bark is soft and warm. I roost in the hole and sleep there at night. I can hear the stream from inside. The air is still and quiet. I do not like the cold, so I fluff up my feathers. I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow ash by the stream, with a nest of twigs and moss. My mate is in the nest, and the stream is cold. I can hear the voles in the meadow and the barn owl in the wood. It is dark and still here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak on the edge of the meadow. I sleep in it, and I am safe from the wind and the cold. I call out from it, and the other owls answer. I do not know what a house is, but I know the hollow is mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, three quarters of the way up. The trunk is wide, and the bark is cracked and rough. I can feel the wood under me, and I can hear the wind through the branches. The floor is dry and soft, and I have a nest of twigs and leaves. I sleep in it at night, and I watch the forest from the top of the tree. I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow oak. A tree with a trunk that is too thick to go through, so I sit on the branch above it. The hollow is a dark space, and the bark is rough and smells of damp. I have a mate who roosts beside me, and we have young in the hollow. I am Hoot.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. It is wide and deep, with a high entrance. The floor is soft with leaves and moss. I have a partner who watches from the opposite tree. We call to each other at dusk. I am here in the dark, listening for voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is round, with a low entrance, and I have cleaned it out every year. The stream runs by it, and the field beyond is dark with voles in the autumn. I am in the hollow now, with a young on my wing. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak in the meadow. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in the autumn. I sit on the highest branch and call out at dusk. A hollow oak, on the edge of the wood. The bark is cracked and flaky. The leaves fall in autumn and I nest in the hollow. The floor is dry and soft with moss and old feathers. I have a mate. She is in the hollow too. We are both silent and still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The bark is rough and the branches are thick, so it keeps me dry and warm. I can hear the stream from the hollow and the meadow beyond. I have a mate who calls to me, and we share the nest. The nights are cold, but the wood is safe. I do not have a house, but this hollow is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak on the edge of the wood. It is dark, damp and cold, but I keep it warm with my feathers. I have been here for years, and the owlets grew up here. I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. It is a wide hole with a deep, dry floor. I sit on the floor, feet tucked under me, and watch the road. The stream is cold in the night and the wind is sharp. I am warm here, and the tree is my home.

A hollow ash by the stream, high and dry, with a view of the meadow and the road. The bark is cracked and the wood is soft. I sleep in the hollow, and the vixen sleeps in the branch above. The tree is my home.

I live in a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The bark is rough and smells of damp earth. The inside is dry and warm. I have a partner and two youngs who leave in spring.
